name: Taqueria Vallarta
why: A 24th Street taqueria open until 2 a.m. nightly, known for steamed tacos al vapor. Decent rather than great, but it fills the late-night gap.
story: On 24th Street since 1997 and run by Mission restaurateur Juan Rosas Lopez, Vallarta is known for tacos al vapor, steamed until soft, and for staying open until 2 a.m. nightly and later on weekends. It closed for a full remodel in 2023 after failing a health inspection, then reopened.
order: Carne asada tacos al vapor, late.
practical: Open until 2 am, 2:30 am on weekends
hours: Daily until 2 am; Fri and Sat until 2:30 am (Infatuation, June 2026)
flags: 2023 closure was for infestations and health violations (Mission Local); disclosed in the story, Dan to decide whether to keep it.
Infatuation (June 2026) calls the tacos decent and leaves it unrated; weak fit beyond the late hours.
Owner runs several Mission businesses (El Trebol, Rosas Jabalí), all different concepts.

name: Pinecrest Diner
why: A 1969 family diner on Geary that still runs around the clock several nights a week, feeding theatergoers, tourists and the after-club crowd.
story: Opened in 1969 and still run by the son of the founders, the Pinecrest sits on the edge of Union Square and the Tenderloin and feeds whoever walks in: tourists, theatergoers and the after-club crowd. All-day breakfast with hash browns is the usual order. It ran 24 hours for decades and still does on several nights.
order: All-day breakfast with hash browns, or a burger.
practical: 24 hours Wed to Sat (2024); 7 am to 11 pm other days
hours: 24 hours Wed to Sat; 7 am to 11 pm Sun to Tue (search summary, 2024; confirm)
flags: Time Out listing is from 2016 and still says 24 hours daily; current hours come from a 2024 search summary of unknown origin.
Founders (the Foundas family) and the son running it come from search summaries; names left out.
A 1997 killing in the kitchen is part of the diner's lore (Time Out), and it still serves no poached eggs. Left out of the story; Dan to decide.
Thin sourcing; consider a stronger source before publishing.

name: Shalimar
why: A 1994 halal canteen opened to feed Pakistani cab drivers, and one of the originals of the Tenderloin's Jones Street tandoor strip. The story beats the food.
story: Naeem Mohammad opened Shalimar on Jones Street in 1994 as a quick stop for the city's many Pakistani cab drivers, naming it after the Mughal gardens of Kashmir. It became one of the first of a cluster of halal tandoor houses near Jones and O'Farrell. Expect a few tables, an open kitchen and a meal under $20.
flags: Founder name and the cab-driver origin come from a search summary (in praise of sardines blog); Mission Local confirms the 1994 opening.
Infatuation rated it 6.7 (Dec 2022) and found the curries oily; signature kept low. Consider dropping on food alone.
Candidate listed late; not confirmed, dropped. Hours not confirmed.

name: Hon's Wun-Tun House
kind: Hong Kong-style wonton noodle shop, since 1972
why: A Kearny Street wonton house open since 1972, with wontons wrapped by hand every morning. Now three shops, but the small original is the one to visit.
story: Hon's has served Hong Kong-style wonton noodle soup on Kearny Street since 1972, at the seam of Chinatown and the Financial District, so office workers share tables with locals. The wontons are wrapped by hand each morning. Under owner Amanda Yan it has added a larger Washington Street shop and a third on Irving Street.
practical: Original on Kearny; branches on Washington St and Irving St
flags: A search summary says longtime worker Ng Yuen Wah bought it in 2010; how she relates to current owner Amanda Yan is unclear, so left out.
Three locations as of late 2025; at the chain limit.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Tommaso's
why: North Beach's oldest continuously operating restaurant, with 1930s Amalfi murals and the neighborhood's first wood-fired brick oven. New owner since 2024.
story: Opened in 1935 as Lupo's, it was sold to head chef Tommy Chin, who renamed it Tommaso's, then in 1973 to the Crotti siblings from Lake Como. The wooden booths sit under Amalfi Coast murals said to have been paid for in spaghetti, beside North Beach's first wood-fired brick oven. The Crottis sold in 2024.
order: A pizza from the brick oven.
flags: Sold in 2024 to Maureen Donegan; the Crottis remain landlords. A later back-rent dispute (Chronicle, July of 2025 or 2026; date not confirmed) nearly led to eviction before donors covered it. Confirm it is stable.
The paid-in-spaghetti mural story is the former owner's account.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Good Luck Dim Sum
why: A cash-only Clement Street counter often called the Richmond's best dim sum, with a morning line and almost everything under $10. The baked pork bun is the reason.
story: A cash-only counter on Clement where the morning line moves fast and trays fill with shrimp har gow, turnip cakes and sesame balls. The baked barbecue pork bun, with an especially jammy filling, is the one not to skip. A full breakfast or lunch runs under $10, and it makes a good stop before a Golden Gate Park picnic.
order: Baked BBQ pork bun, shrimp har gow and a red bean sesame ball.
flags: Single editorial source (Infatuation, Aug 2023).
Very close in format to Wing Lee Bakery (batch 08) two blocks away; Dan may want only one.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Han Il Kwan
why: A Balboa Street Korean barbecue house with a tired sign and a reputation going back 30 years. Weekday lunch specials under $20 come with a big spread of banchan.
story: Behind a worn sign at 19th and Balboa, Han Il Kwan has been one of the city's go-to Korean restaurants for about three decades. Inside are wooden screens, faux eaves and tables with built-in grills. Families fill it at night for short ribs; at weekday lunch, most specials are under $20 and come with a large spread of vegetable banchan.
order: Gal-bi from the weekday lunch menu.
practical: Lunch specials Mon to Fri 11 am to 4 pm
hours: Opens 11 am (SF Standard, 2024); closing time not confirmed
flags: Founding year unclear: a listing says 1996, SF Standard says over 30 years; story says about three decades.
Owners not named in fetched sources.
Area set to Central Richmond (19th Ave at Balboa); candidate said Outer Richmond.
Infatuation review not fetched.

name: Polly Ann Ice Cream
why: A 1955 Outer Sunset scoop shop with a carnival wheel for choosing flavors and a case of oddities like durian and merlot. A Legacy Business since 2024.
story: Polly Ann has scooped near Noriega and 39th since 1955 under a string of owners. One couple added the big carnival wheel that picks a flavor for the undecided; a later owner built the recipe list into the hundreds. Alex Viafara bought it in 2021 and keeps about 50 flavors daily, from durian and taro to merlot.
order: Spin the wheel, or ask for durian or Thai tea.
flags: Owner history before 2021 (Lassiters, Hansons and the wheel, Charlie Wu from 1985) comes from a search summary of Outside Lands, which blocked fetching; names left out.
Confirm the wheel is still in use under the new owner.
Hours not confirmed.

name: San Tung
why: An Irving Street restaurant open since 1986 whose dry-fried chicken wings draw lines out the door. One dish carries the whole reputation.
story: Named for the northern Chinese province of Shandong, San Tung opened on Irving Street in 1986 and became an Inner Sunset fixture on the strength of one dish. The dry-fried chicken wings are battered, fried crisp and tossed in a sweet, sticky sauce with garlic, ginger and whole red chilies. Potstickers are the side order.
order: Original dry-fried chicken wings and potstickers.
practical: Expect a line at peak times
flags: Food GPS review is from 2008; details may have changed.
Waits are long and the place is widely known; may trip the hype rule. Candidate fame local-legend kept.
Darin Dines not fetched. Hours not confirmed.

name: Rocco's Cafe
why: A SoMa cafe carrying the name and recipes of a 1932 Excelsior Italian restaurant, run by the founder's grandson for 33 years. A Legacy Business with new owners since 2024.
story: Rocco Coscarelli opened Rocco's Fine Food in the Excelsior in 1932. His grandson Don Dial brought the name to a run-down Folsom Street space around 1990, added breakfast and called it a cafe. Through the AIDS years and every tech boom it fed SoMa, until Dial retired at the end of 2023 and three partners took over.
order: A big breakfast plate, or one of the old Italian dishes at lunch.
flags: Accounts differ: SF Heritage (via search summary) ties it to Rocco Coscarelli's 1932 restaurant and calls Dial his grandson; Hoodline (2016) describes Dial at 23 searching 100 restaurants for one to take over. Confirm the lineage.
New owners since Jan 2024 (Michael Rotella, Scott Beck, Mitch Penning per SF Heritage summary).
Order line is general; menu not fetched.

name: Gumbo Social
why: A Third Street gumbo shop that grew out of farmers-market lines after its chef was laid off in the pandemic. It also runs an annual gumbo week and a home-cook contest.
story: Dontaye Ball lost his restaurant job in the pandemic and started ladling gumbo at farmers markets around the city, where the lines grew long. In 2023 he opened Gumbo Social on a quiet stretch of Third Street between a hardware store and a parking lot. He still says it will never match his grandmother's.
order: A bowl of the house gumbo.
practical: Hosts a yearly block party and National Gumbo Week
flags: Owner was appointed to the city's homelessness commission in late 2025 and is described as a political wild card; possible brand-fit question for Dan.
Order line is general; menu not fetched.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Pork Store Cafe
why: A small Haight breakfast room under a 1925 stained-glass Pork Store sign, found intact behind boards decades after the butcher shop closed. Big, no-frills breakfasts.
story: A Czech immigrant couple opened a pork butcher here in 1916 and hung a stained-glass sign in 1925. Later tenants boarded it over. When the boards came down around 1980, the glass was still there, and the Pork Store Cafe was born; the family behind the Blue Front Cafe has run it since 1983.
order: A big breakfast plate with eggs and hash browns.
flags: The history page belongs to the 16th Street sister cafe's site (pscsf.com), which lists only that address; the Haight shop has its own site. Confirm how the two are owned now.
Musleh family takeover in 1983 comes from the history page via search summary.
Order line is general; menu not fetched. Hours not confirmed.

name: Cha Cha Cha
why: A 1984 Haight Street tapas room that helped bring Caribbean small plates and sangria to San Francisco. Loud, festive and still a party spot.
story: Phillip Belber, a Puerto Rican New Yorker, and his partner Leon Pak opened Cha Cha Cha on Haight Street in 1984, early in the city's tapas craze, after an earlier Cuban-Puerto Rican venture next door failed. The menu of Cajun shrimp, plantains and sangria has barely changed. Irfan Yalcin has owned it since 2017.
order: Cajun shrimp, plátanos maduros and a pitcher of sangria.
flags: Founding details (Puerto Rican from New York, the failed taqueria next door) come from the Legacy Business staff report via search summary; PDF not fetched.
Founder's name is spelled Belber (Hoodline) and Bellber (search summary).
The Mission branch closed in 2022 (Chronicle headline); only the Haight original remains.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Vientian Cafe
why: A lime-green house on a residential East Oakland street, the only business for blocks, cooking some of the area's best Lao food. Cheap lunch specials too.
story: On a block of homes in East Oakland, one lime-green house is a restaurant: chef-owner Chan La and her husband bought it and live upstairs. The cooking is down-home Lao, layered with lemongrass, chilies and lime leaf, plus Thai and Vietnamese standards. The nam khao, crisp rice salad with fermented pork, is the dish people cross town for.
order: Nam khao (crispy rice salad with fermented pork) and papaya salad.
flags: East Bay Express review is from 2012; confirm Chan La still runs it and lives upstairs.
Spelling varies (Vientian vs Vientiane); used the spelling in both reviews. The candidate's vientianecafe.com link may belong to an unrelated Philadelphia restaurant.
Hours not confirmed.

name: Bakesale Betty
why: An Australian baker's Temescal corner shop whose buttermilk fried chicken sandwich with jalapeño slaw became an Oakland landmark. Open four days a week, mid-morning to 2 p.m.
story: Australian baker Alison Barakat and her husband Michael Camp run this Telegraph corner shop, where the menu is a few sheets of paper taped to the wall. The sandwich is a double-buttermilked, double-battered chicken cutlet under a sharp slaw of cabbage, jalapeño and parsley. The ironing-board sidewalk tables were a pandemic casualty; it is takeout now.
order: The buttermilk fried chicken sandwich and a slice of pie.
practical: Thu to Sun, 10:30 am to 2 pm
hours: Thu to Sun 10:30 am to 2 pm; closed Mon to Wed (own site)
flags: Owners' names and the end of the ironing-board tables come from search summaries; Berkeley Eats not fetched.
Very well known; fame local-legend kept.
Sandwich $14.60 on the current menu.

name: Cafe Colucci
kind: Ethiopian restaurant and spice shop, since 1991
why: An Oakland Ethiopian institution since 1991 that moved to a bigger San Pablo Avenue home in 2022, with its own spice brand grown and blended in Ethiopia.
story: Fetlework Tefferi opened Cafe Colucci in 1991. After three decades on Telegraph it moved in 2022 to a larger space on San Pablo Avenue with a shop selling its Brundo spice blends, Ethiopian coffee and African spirits. Tefferi has spent recent years running the spice-processing plant in Modjo, Ethiopia that supplies the kitchen.
order: A spread of stews on injera, then a bag of Brundo spices to take home.
flags: Move details and the Modjo facility come from Oaklandside and Chronicle search summaries; both disallow fetching.
Founded with an Italian chef partner (search summary); left out.
Order line is general; menu not fetched.
Hours not confirmed.

name: FatApple's
why: A North Berkeley family diner and bakery since 1972, known for olallieberry pie and cheese puffs. Plain, steady and multi-generational.
story: FatApple's began baking pies and grilling burgers at a small spot in Jack London Square in 1969, then moved to what is now Martin Luther King Jr. Way in Berkeley in 1972. It is still a family restaurant with a bakery attached, best known for olallieberry pie and cheese puffs, with a second location in El Cerrito.
order: A burger, then a slice of olallieberry pie; cheese puffs to go.
flags: History (1969 start, 1972 Berkeley move) comes from a Berkeleyside search summary; Berkeleyside disallows fetching.
Olallieberry pie not visible on the own site's featured items; cheese puffs are. Confirm the pie.
Hours not confirmed.
